questions.q: What happens when RAM becomes full and another program is opened?
options: Data that is not in use is moved out to secondary storage to make room
The computer switches itself off to protect the data
The CPU reduces its clock speed until space is free
The oldest file on the hard disk is deleted
questions.feedback: Something is moved out rather than lost. The space it moves to is virtual memory.

questions.q: State what is meant by virtual memory.

markPoints.concept: secondary storage used as if it were extra RAM
accept: as if|like|extra ram|more ram|pretend|instead of ram|acts as|additional memory|extra memory|more memory|used as memory
markPoints.exemplar: Part of secondary storage used as if it were extra RAM.

questions.example: A part of secondary storage that is used as if it were extra RAM.
questions.paraphrase: Space on the drive that the computer treats as additional memory.
questions.feedback: It is storage behaving as memory, not a separate kind of chip.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.2 Lesson 2 — Swap space, station 1: When RAM runs out

questions.q: Explain why a computer that is using virtual memory heavily feels slow.

markPoints.concept: data has to be moved between RAM and secondary storage
markPoints.exemplar: Data is moved between RAM and secondary storage.

markPoints.concept: secondary storage is much slower to access than RAM
markPoints.exemplar: Secondary storage is much slower to read than RAM.

markPoints.concept: so the CPU waits for data and the programs run more slowly
markPoints.exemplar: This means the CPU is left waiting, so the program runs more slowly.

questions.example: When RAM is full, data is constantly moved between RAM and secondary storage. Secondary storage is far slower to read and write than RAM, so the CPU spends time waiting for data to arrive and the programs run noticeably more slowly.
questions.paraphrase: The computer keeps shuffling data out to the drive and back, and because the drive is much slower than memory the processor is held up and everything drags.
questions.feedback: Three ideas: the moving, the speed difference, and what that does to the program. The third needs to be joined to the second.
questions.hint: What is being moved, how fast is the place it moves to, and what is the CPU doing meanwhile?
questions.revisitLabel: 1.2 Lesson 2 — Swap space, station 4: Why it's slow

questions.q: Which of these would reduce how much a computer relies on virtual memory?
questions.feedback: Virtual memory is used because RAM ran out, so more RAM is what stops it. A bigger disk just gives more room for the swapping to happen in.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.2 Lesson 2 — Swap space, station 4: Why it's slow

questions.q: Which of these would help a computer avoid using virtual memory? Tick all that apply.
options: Closing programs that are not being used
Choosing programs that need less memory
correct: Closing programs that are not being used
Choosing programs that need less memory
questions.feedback: Anything that keeps what is needed inside RAM. A faster CPU does not change how much memory a program asks for.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.2 Lesson 2 — Swap space, station 5: Avoiding virtual memory

questions.q: State one sign that a computer is relying on virtual memory.

markPoints.concept: it becomes noticeably slower, and the drive is busy
markPoints.exemplar: It becomes much slower to respond.

questions.example: Everything becomes much slower, and the drive is busy even though nothing is being saved.
questions.paraphrase: The machine starts dragging and the disk light stays on.
questions.feedback: Slowness is the symptom everybody notices; the busy drive is the one that says why.
